title: How Does a Clam Eat Through Wood? 🪵
description:
How does a shipworm eat wood? This clam grinds tunnels with two tiny shell plates, then relies on bacteria in its gills to make the enzymes that digest the wood.

Sources:
https://news.northeastern.edu/2022/11/23/how-do-shipworms-eat/
https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1347687-gill-bacteria-enable-novel-digestive-strategy-wood-feeding-mollusk
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/tunneling-clam-bedeviled-humans-sank-ships-conquered-oceans-180961288/

topic: How does a clam (the shipworm) eat through wood?
script:
This clam can eat your wooden boat,
and you'd never guess how.
It's called a shipworm.
It looks like a worm, but it's really a clam.
Its shell? Just two tiny plates on its head.
It grinds them into wood like a rasp
and tunnels deeper as it grows.
The sawdust goes straight to its stomach.
But there's a problem.
Wood is really hard to digest.
So the shipworm keeps helpers in its gills.
Bacteria that make wood-melting enzymes.
They send those enzymes down to the gut,
and the clam turns timber into food.
Its tail stays at the hole, breathing seawater.
That's how shipworms chewed through wooden ships for centuries.
Sailors called them the termites of the sea.
So which would you rather find in your boat?
Termites, or a hungry clam?
key_facts: Their shell is reduced to two small plates at the head, used to bore into wood
Bacteria living in the gills make wood-digesting enzymes that are carried to the gut
They keep their tail siphons at the entrance hole to the seawater
Shipworms have damaged wooden ships for centuries and are called termites of the sea
